key: Amplitude does not change the color. Color is set by the wavelength.
alt: Left, three red waves drawn one above the other over the same distance, marked Distance traveled in 1 second. The top wave has long wavelength, lambda 1, and frequency nu 1 = 3 cycles per second = 3 hertz. The middle wave has a shorter wavelength, lambda 2, and nu 2 = 6 cycles per second = 6 hertz. The bottom wave has the shortest wavelength, lambda 3, and nu 3 = 12 cycles per second = 12 hertz. Right, two waves with the same wavelength but different heights: a taller one labeled Higher amplitude and a flatter one labeled Lower amplitude, with the amplitude, a, marked as the height of a crest above the middle line.
caption: The parts of a wave. Left: all three waves travel the same distance in 1 second, so the wave with the shortest wavelength has the most crests passing each second, the highest frequency. Right: two waves with the same wavelength (same color of light) but different amplitudes; the taller wave is the brighter light.
why: Shows wavelength, frequency and amplitude, and their inverse relation, which 3.1 describes only in words.

key: so chemists can identify elements by the light they give off
alt: Five spectra stacked on one wavelength scale running from 4000 to 7000 angstroms (400 to 700 nanometers). The top row, white light, is a smooth, unbroken rainbow from violet at the left through blue, green, yellow and orange to red at the right. Below it, four black strips each show only a few thin colored lines. Sodium, Na: two blue-green lines near 4980 angstroms, a few yellow lines, the brightest a thick yellow pair near 5890 angstroms, and one orange line. Hydrogen, H: four lines, violet near 4100, violet near 4340, blue-green near 4860 and red near 6560 angstroms. Calcium, Ca: many lines, several violet and blue, some green and yellow, and red lines. Mercury, Hg: violet, blue, blue-green, green, yellow, orange and red lines in a different pattern.
caption: A continuous spectrum (white light, top) compared with the line spectra of sodium, hydrogen, calcium and mercury. Each element gives its own pattern of lines. The scale is in angstroms (1 Å = 0.1 nm, so 4000 Å = 400 nm). Sodium’s bright yellow lines near 589 nm are the yellow-orange of a salt flame.
why: Real side-by-side continuous vs. line spectra for four elements; our Bohr SVG shows only hydrogen, and it ties to the salt-flame opener.

key: So the largest atoms are at the lower left of the table
lead: Plotting atomic radius against atomic number shows both trends at once: the radius jumps up at the start of each new period and falls across it.
alt: Line graph titled Atomic Radii: radius in picometers, 0 to 300, versus atomic number, 0 to 60. The line makes a repeating sawtooth. Each tall peak is an alkali metal, labeled in purple: Li about 150 pm, Na about 185, K about 227, Rb about 248 and Cs about 265. After each peak the line falls across the period to a low point at a noble gas, labeled in blue: He about 32 pm, Ne about 70, Ar about 98, Kr about 112 and Xe about 130. Two red circles mark the period 4 and period 5 transition elements, where the radius stays nearly flat, between about 125 and 160 pm.
caption: Atomic radius versus atomic number. Each period starts with a large alkali metal and shrinks toward its noble gas, and every peak is higher than the one before because a new shell has been added. The radii change only a little across the transition elements.
why: Real data graph for the radius trend; 3.6 has only our arrow diagram.

key: so the electrons repel each other more and the cloud spreads out
alt: Spheres drawn to scale with their radii. Aluminum atom, Al, a green sphere, 118. Aluminum ion, Al3+, a much smaller brown sphere, 68. Sulfur atom, S, a green sphere, 104. Sulfide ion, S2-, a much larger brown sphere, 170.
caption: Atoms and their ions drawn to scale (radii in picometers). Losing three electrons shrinks aluminum from 118 to 68 pm; gaining two electrons swells sulfur from 104 to 170 pm.
why: Shows to scale, with numbers, that cations shrink and anions grow.

lead: Because every ion in an ionic solid is attracted to all the ions around it, ionic compounds are hard solids with high melting points; sodium chloride melts at 801 °C. Solid NaCl does not conduct electricity, because its ions are locked in place. Once it melts (or dissolves in water), the ions are free to move and carry a current. A molecular compound such as sugar has no ions, so a sugar solution does not conduct.
alt: Three photographs joined by arrows. First, a small crucible of white solid sits on a ring stand, wired into a circuit with a light bulb; the bulb is off. Second, a Bunsen burner flame heats the crucible from below and the solid begins to melt; the bulb is still off. Third, the solid has melted and the light bulb is glowing brightly.
caption: Solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity, but molten NaCl does: once the ions can move, they complete the circuit and the bulb lights.
credit_extra: photos: modification of work by Mark Blaser and Matt Evans
why: Real evidence that ionic compounds are made of ions; 4.1 has only a particle diagram.

lead: Aluminum oxide, Al2O3, the first swap-drop example, is a real and useful compound. As the mineral corundum it is one of the hardest natural substances. A trace of iron and titanium ions turns it blue (sapphire), and a trace of chromium(III) ions turns it red (ruby). Clear, lab-grown sapphire is also used to make the nearly invisible ceramic brackets on some braces.
alt: A gold ring set with a large oval, faceted blue gemstone held by small gold prongs.
caption: A blue sapphire is aluminum oxide, Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>. Pure aluminum oxide is colorless; traces of iron and titanium give sapphire its blue color.
credit_extra: photo: modification of work by Stanislav Doronenko via Wikipedia
why: Gives the Al2O3 swap-drop example an everyday object, with a dental (orthodontics) tie.

lead: Mineral sunscreens show both kinds of metal side by side. Zinc oxide, ZnO, needs no Roman numeral, because zinc is always 2+. Titanium is a transition metal that can form more than one ion, so TiO2 needs one: two O2− ions put 4− on the scale, so the titanium is 4+, and the name is titanium(IV) oxide. (On sunscreen labels it is listed by its common name, titanium dioxide.)
alt: Two images. (a) A hand spreading thick white sunscreen on a person’s lower leg. (b) A ball-and-stick model of a titanium dioxide crystal: gray titanium atoms and red oxygen atoms in a repeating three-dimensional network, with twice as many oxygen atoms as titanium atoms.
caption: (a) Titanium(IV) oxide, TiO<sub>2</sub>, is the white compound in many mineral sunscreens. (b) In its crystal, titanium and oxygen are present in a 1 : 2 ratio, the ratio the formula gives.
credit_extra: photo a: modification of work by “osseous”/Flickr
why: Everyday health product that practices the Roman-numeral rule and contrasts it with fixed-charge zinc.

key: is the acid in vinegar (about 5% in water)
alt: Three images. (a) A plastic jug of distilled white vinegar. (b) The structural formula of acetic acid: a carbon with three H atoms bonded to a second carbon, which has a double bond to one O and a single bond to an O that carries an H. (c) A ball-and-stick model of the same molecule, with black carbon, red oxygen and white hydrogen atoms.
caption: (a) Vinegar is a dilute solution of acetic acid. (b, c) Of the four H atoms in acetic acid, only the one bonded to oxygen is released as H<sup>+</sup>; that is why the formula is written HC<sub>2</sub>H<sub>3</sub>O<sub>2</sub> or CH<sub>3</sub>COOH, with the acidic H set apart.
credit_extra: photo a: modification of work by “HomeSpot HQ”/Flickr
why: Everyday acid photo plus structure that explains the odd HC2H3O2 formula taught in 4.5.
